description: We're University Students from Nagpur building something that actually makes an impact.
summary: Cratera is a web app that helps mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates at the Moon’s south pole. At the pole the Sun hugs the horizon and Earth sits low in the sky, so a single ridge can cut off a lander’s power or its direct line to Earth. Cratera combines NASA LOLA terrain data with JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions to show where each body sits relative to a site’s real terrain horizon. Users pick a site on a Moon globe and a date, and see sunlight and Earth-visibility windows, time until sunset and Earthset, and side-by-side comparisons of other sites or dates. It answers the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by turning expert-only data from tools like Quickmap, Moon Trek and Horizons into a fast, intuitive what-if planner. This matters because missions often slip, and planners need to re-evaluate sites and dates quickly to keep power and communication safe.
details:
What it does and how it works
Cratera answers one question: for a chosen south pole site and date, when are the Sun and Earth actually visible? We built it in two stages. First, an offline pipeline reads NASA’s LOLA south pole elevation model and, for each site, traces rays along all 360 compass directions out to 60 km. It includes the Moon’s curvature, finds the highest terrain angle in each direction, and saves a 360-value horizon profile. Second, JPL Horizons gives the Sun’s and Earth’s azimuth and elevation over time for each site. In the browser, a body counts as visible only if its elevation is above the terrain horizon at its azimuth. The results are small static files, so the site is fast and needs no backend or API key. The app covers six south pole sites: Shackleton Rim, Connecting Ridge, Malapert Mountain, Haworth Rim, Nobile Rim and de Gerlache Rim & also 2 Apollo sites Apollo11 and Apollo17.

Benefits and intended impact
Cratera makes lunar lighting and communication analysis quick and understandable. A mission team facing a launch delay can see in seconds how a new date or a backup site changes power and Earth contact. It also works as an educational tool, showing students and the public why the south pole is so difficult.

Tools, languages and software

  • Terrain pipeline: Python with NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj and Matplotlib
  • Data: NASA LRO LOLA elevation models (PGDA) and JPL Horizons
  • Website: Next.js, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, [Plotly / D3 / Three.js], hosted on Vercel
  • AI tools: AI Studio & Antigravity helped with coding and writing; the team chose the parameters and sites, reviewed and tested the results, and made all commits. See AI_USAGE.md in our repository.
  • No special hardware was used.

What is creative about it
Most tools show Sun and Earth positions over a flat horizon. Cratera uses each site’s real horizon, so a ridge that blocks the Sun is visible and counted. The result is presented in one place, with side-by-side comparison designed for quick decisions, not detailed analysis.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: the Moon’s curvature, the polar grid’s difference from compass north (we corrected for it), and a cross-check between the 80 m and 40 m terrain data, which agreed to about 0.18° on average at Shackleton.
  • Speed and accessibility: precomputed static data, so it runs on any device.
  • Honesty about limits: rays stop at 60 km, the Sun is treated as a point, and the terrain data covers only 80°S to 90°S, so equatorial sites such as the Apollo landing sites are not included.
  • Future work: custom coordinates, a 3D terrain view and more sites.
